question: A marketing team has always written its weekly client status note by hand. They now plan to switch to a new arrangement in which Claude drafts the note each week and an account manager edits it before sending. Before the first Claude-drafted note under the new arrangement reaches a client, what should the team do first?
options: A) Agree in advance exactly how many minutes of editing per note the account manager should expect to spend on this every week.
B) Send the first Claude-drafted note straight to the client, along with a short note explaining that Claude helped produce it.
C) Run Claude on a past month's inputs and compare its drafts with the hand-written notes actually sent to clients that month.
D) Ask Claude to check its own draft against the account manager's usual style before it goes out to the client.
correct_answers: C) Run Claude on a past month's inputs and compare its drafts with the hand-written notes actually sent to clients that month.
explanations: An editing-time budget measures effort, which only means something once the drafts are known to be usable. Agreeing on one before that check risks pressuring the account manager to spend less time editing than the drafts actually need.

Disclosure is good practice, but it does not test anything the team needs to know yet. The client would still receive the first output of an arrangement nobody has tried, and explaining that Claude helped does not make an inaccurate status note acceptable.

Correct. Feeding Claude the same weekly inputs the account manager already used, for a month that has already happened, produces drafts the team can check against a known right answer: the hand-written note the client actually received that week, before Claude was involved. That lets the team see where Claude's drafts fall short before any client sees output from the new arrangement.

Self-review can catch obvious slips, but Claude judging its own draft uses the same understanding that produced the draft in the first place. That is no substitute for comparing drafts against notes the team already knows were accurate.
